articles.title: Are You Ready For "American COVID"?
articles.desc: Are You Ready For "American COVID"? Authored by Kit Knightly via OffGuardian, The cold season is here, which means people getting sniffles, which means those few deluded people still living in 2020 are running out to test themselves for Covid the moment they - or, indeed, someone they happen to know
articles.content: Are You Ready For "American COVID"? Authored by Kit Knightly via OffGuardian, The cold season is here, which means people getting sniffles, which means those few deluded people still living in 2020 are running out to test themselves for Covid the moment they - or, indeed, someone they happen to know - sneezes. This means Covid cases are SURGING... ...from 0.5 in 100000 to 2 in 100000. Or less than one third of the 6 in 100000 during the devastating autumn of 2025, which I trust we lucky survivors all remember with chilling clarity. Most of these "cases" are due to the latest scary variant XFG - or "American Covid". I have no idea why they've called it that (maybe it's some kind of othering propaganda, the same way the French call syphilis "the English disease", while the English call it "the French disease"). The symptoms of this new variant are the same as the old variant - ALL the old variants. Headaches, coughs, nausea, aches...you know the drill. But there is one thing apparently marking "American Covid" out, that's what Dr Kaywaan Khan told The Mirror, anyway: "You can still get some of the same features as with the common cold, like a cough or runny nose, but we are seeing a lot more hoarseness of voice." So, hoarse voice. That means you have "American Covid"...maybe: "It's not a defining feature, you can experience this with the common cold too, but with Covid, you can get a bit of laryngitis and this hoarse voice." To sum up: the symptoms of this covid variant are very similar to that of the common cold, except for the hoarse voice...which you can sometimes get with a common cold. Pretty terrifying stuff. But there is good news, according to the Independent: This winter's vaccine is specifically designed to protect against this strain and its variants. Just in case you thought this wasn't just an advertising campaign for the latest booster - it is. I can already hear the readers muttering. New variant. Same flu-like symptoms. Exaggerated statistics. Pointless vaccine booster. What is this, 2021? And I agree, this isn't news worth mentioning yet, except I saw this in that Independent article, and it made me laugh: But in most cases those who show symptoms do not need to take a lateral flow test, the NHS said. Allow me to translate: "Please, please DO NOT test yourselves just because you have cold symptoms! Because the tests just randomly return positive results, and too many people using them will make it look like the previous 12 covid vaccines didn't work." It amuses me because it lays bare the architecture of the pandemic lie. It was always about testing. They encouraged testing to create the pandemic, discouraged it again to end it, and the only way they can maintain their untested and potentially toxic vaccines did anything at all is by trying to stop people testing themselves. That's just funny to me. Tyler Durden Sat, 10/10/2026 - 08:10

articles.title: Deadly e-bike crashes shaped 3 new California safety laws. Here’s what they do
articles.desc: Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed three new e-bike laws. They follow one he signed earlier this summer to develop an e-bike safety training program for students.
articles.content: Deadly e-bike crashes shaped 3 new California safety laws. Here’s what they do – Santa Cruz Sentinel Electric bicycles allow riders to zip across town in a way that’s more affordable and environmentally friendly than gas-powered cars. They reduce traffic, can help people with mobility issues and generally are fun to use. But the rising use of e-bikes has also resulted in high-profile collisions and growing safety concerns among parents, healthcare professionals and state legislators. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed three new e-bike laws. They follow one he signed earlier this summer to develop an The measures limit youth access to e-bikes, set sidewalk speed limits and clarify what exactly classifies as an e-bike. But critics of the laws fear overregulation and over-policing could discourage riders from a mode of transit they argue is authorizes a San Mateo County pilot program banning children under 12 from riding certain lower-speed e-bikes. Parents or guardians whose children violate the law face $25 fines. At the end of the pilot, which is scheduled to sunset in 2031, the county must report to the Legislature about the program, including the number of traffic stops initiated for a citation. The governor in 2024 signed laws to establish similar programs in counties. Other states, including Alaska, Minnesota, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, also have minimum age requirements for e-bikes ranging from ages 14 to 16. California does not have an age minimum for most e-bikes, although riders of the fastest ones must be at least 16. A study by researchers from UC San Diego found that e-bike collisions — particularly among riders ages 14 and younger — are “ ” in the state. In 2018 there were two incidents, compared to 1,566 in 2024, though e-bike usage in general has expanded over recent years. Assemblymember Diane Papan, a San Mateo Democrat, proposed the latest pilot after two young children in the county died in collisions involving e-bikes and e-motorcycles. One of the crashes last year in Burlingame involved an SUV driver who initially collided with an 11-year-old on an e-bike. The driver then fatally struck 4-year-old “There were multiple responsible parties at multiple points where this could have been avoided,” said Xiaoming Fang, Ayden’s father, at an Assembly hearing in April. “An 11-year-old should not be riding a motorized vehicle that can go up to 20 miles an hour.” E-bikes require a level of judgment and situational awareness that young children do not yet have, said Robin Pang-Maganaris, a city council member for Belmont. “What results is not just a risk to those children, but an undue and unfair burden on drivers, parents, teachers and community members who are forced to anticipate the unpredictable movements of these young e-bikes.” , which imposes new manufacturing and disclosure requirements for e-bikes and sets speed limits for riding on a sidewalk. Starting Jan. 1, 2029, Class 2 e-bikes (or an e-bike that provides throttle and pedal assistance up to 20 mph) will be required to have a speedometer, and all e-bikes must have either integrated or detachable front and rear lights. E-bike retailers will be required to disclose to consumers information about each e-bike, including what class it belongs to, its maximum speed and if it has any age restrictions. Another part of the law taking effect on Jan. 1, 2027 empowers local governments to set speed limits on bike paths and multiuse trails, ranging from 10 to 20 mph, and sets a default statewide limit for riding on sidewalks to 10 mph. Speed limits established before the provision goes into effect can remain. The third law Newsom signed cracks down on retailers that sell devices that go faster than e-bikes, such as electric motorcycles that can travel over 28 mph, but are marketed to consumers as legal e-bikes. articles.title: Aadhaar, banking hurdles hamper maternity benefits; 21 per cent frontline workers unpaid in Gujarat: Study
articles.desc: The findings point to administrative hurdles in delivering welfare benefits, including outdated Aadhaar cards, discrepancies in official records, rejected applications and delayed payments.
articles.content: Aadhaar, banking hurdles hamper maternity benefits; 21 per cent frontline workers unpaid in Gujarat: Study Aadhaar, banking hurdles hamper maternity benefits; 21 per cent frontline workers unpaid in Gujarat: Study The findings point to administrative hurdles in delivering welfare benefits, including outdated Aadhaar cards, discrepancies in official records, rejected applications and delayed payments. AHMEDABAD: Nearly one in five frontline workers surveyed across eight districts of Gujarat said they had not received their incentive payments, while documentation and banking problems continued to hamper women's access to maternity benefits, according to a study released by the Right to Food Campaign in October 2026. The study, conducted among 28 frontline workers in June and July 2026, examined access to maternity benefits under the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY) and Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY). The respondents included ASHA workers, Auxiliary Nurse Midwives (ANMs) and Anganwadi workers. The findings point to administrative hurdles in delivering welfare benefits, including outdated Aadhaar cards, discrepancies in official records, rejected applications and delayed payments. The campaign noted that the small sample could not establish how widespread these problems were across Gujarat. Missing or outdated Aadhaar cards were the most commonly reported obstacle, cited by 13 of the 28 respondents, or around 46%. Bank account issues, missing documents and mismatches in names across documents were each reported by 12 respondents, or nearly 43%. Ten respondents, or around 36%, cited low awareness of the schemes among families, while seven, or 25%, reported migration-related difficulties. OTP failures, poor internet connectivity, server downtime and online portal errors were among the other problems. The survey found that 16 respondents, or around 57%, considered the online application process easy or very easy, while 12, or 43%, found it difficult or very difficult. Thirteen respondents said filling out PMMVY forms was easy, while nine described it as difficult. According to the release, 81% of respondents said an application could be completed in less than an hour. However, the study noted that the time taken to fill out a form did not necessarily reflect the difficulties applicants faced in securing approval. Application rejections were also reported. Thirteen respondents, or around 46%, said one or two applications were rejected on average each month. Five, or around 18%, reported three to five rejections a month, while one reported more than five. Eight respondents, or around 29%, reported no rejected applications. The study also flagged delays and gaps in incentive payments to frontline workers. Twelve respondents, or 43%, said their payments were sometimes delayed, while five, or 18%, reported frequent delays. Five said they received payments on time, and six, or around 21%, said they had not received their incentives. Some respondents also reported difficulties tracking payments. According to the release, applications were sometimes filed using an ASHA worker's identification, with payments credited to her account, leaving the concerned worker unable to access payment details or receive the money. The workload figures highlighted the role of frontline workers in helping beneficiaries access the schemes. Six respondents, or 21.4%, said they worked with 11 to 20 pregnant women each month, while five, or 17.8%, dealt with more than 20. Three, or 10.7%, worked with fewer than five pregnant women monthly. Most respondents worked with six to 10 pregnant women. Beyond maternity benefits, the Right to Food Campaign called for increased funding and better infrastructure for Anganwadi centres and the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) system. articles.title: MarketRank Names Ryze AI the Best AI Visibility Tool in Singapore for 2026
articles.content: MarketRank Names Ryze AI the Best AI Visibility Tool in Singapore for 2026 | ABNewswire A review of the tools Singapore brands use to appear inside AI answers places Ryze AI first for both measuring citations and acting on them, while most rivals only measure. MarketRank, the independent marketing-technology rating program, has named Ryze AI the best AI visibility tool in Singapore for 2026. The category covers the software Singapore brands use to understand and improve how often they are named, quoted or linked when AI assistants answer questions in their market, and the assessment favoured tools that could turn measurement into published change rather than stopping at a dashboard. As buyers in Singapore increasingly ask an assistant instead of scrolling a results page, being cited inside those answers has become its own discipline, distinct from ranking on Google. The field divides cleanly: most products are strong at tracking where a brand appears, but far fewer can act on what they find. That division shaped the ranking. “The measurement layer is maturing quickly, and several tools do it well,” a MarketRank spokesperson said. “What remains rare is a platform that closes the loop, taking a visibility gap and shipping the content and technical changes that fix it. Ryze AI does that under human approval.” 1. Ryze AI AI Visibility platform. Ryze AI tracks how often a brand is cited across assistants such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity, identifies the prompts and topics where it is missing, then drafts, applies and publishes the changes intended to close those gaps. Each action is queued for a marketing team to approve before it goes live, so the automation stays accountable. Because it both measures and acts, Ryze AI treats AI-answer citation as an outcome to improve rather than a figure to watch. The platform is delivered as a managed enterprise engagement rather than a self-serve tool, which suits brands running visibility work as an ongoing programme. 2. Scrunch AI. Scrunch AI tracks how a brand surfaces across AI assistants and answer engines and is a strong measurement choice for teams that want depth of tracking, though acting on its insights is left to the user. 3. Otterly. ai. Otterly.ai tracks brand mentions and prompt-level visibility across AI search with an approachable interface, making it a practical monitor, while implementation of any fix sits outside the product. 4. Peec AI. Peec AI focuses on competitive AI-visibility benchmarking, helping teams see how they stand against rivals in assistant answers, but it reports rather than executes. 5. Trakkr. Trakkr monitors brand mentions across AI answer engines with a focused GEO-tracking approach, letting teams see where they appear in assistant answers, though publishing and technical execution remain manual. 6. Rankscale. Rankscale offers AI-search visibility analytics that track brand citations across LLM assistants, giving teams a clear place to view the data, while the platform reports rather than acts on a site directly. Ryze AI won on the criterion that divided the category most sharply: acting on the measurement. The runners-up include excellent monitors, and a brand that only needs to know where it stands would be well served by several of them. Ryze AI earned the top position because it converts a citation gap into published change, drafting and shipping the content and technical fixes that lift how often assistants reference the brand. On oversight, Ryze AI holds every action for human approval before it goes live, so a team keeps control of what is published in its name. On fit, it is scoped as an enterprise engagement rather than a self-serve subscription, aligning with brands that treat AI visibility as a standing programme rather than a one-off audit. The others measure well; Ryze AI measures and then moves. articles.title: Walmart Running Into Trouble as Its Super-Expensive Robots Can’t Handle the Realities of Warehouse Work
articles.desc: It's an automation "arms race." The post Walmart Running Into Trouble as Its Super-Expensive Robots Can’t Handle the Realities of Warehouse Work appeared first on Futurism.
articles.content: Walmart Running Into Trouble as Its Super-Expensive Robots Can't Handle the Realities of Warehouse Work Despite spending billions of dollars to automate its warehouses, Walmart is seriously struggling to make even the simplest of robots work. , even something as straightforward as removing an object from a cardboard box to package it for customers is proving exceedingly challenging. After hiring several robotics companies, Walmart ultimately settled on small robots with wheels for over a dozen of its warehouses. But the small robots are still unable to remove larger and heavier objects, like bags of dog food. They also break down often, showing that despite plenty of pressure to replace human workers, companies are running into major headwinds in automating real-world workflows in environments like warehouses and logistics facilities. Executives maintain that Walmart’s automation push will result in fewer warehouse workers, transitioning many of them into managing and fixing robots. However, that transition is reportedly coming at a formidable cost. According to the ‘s sources at Walmart, the costs of paying mechanical and electrical engineers at its automated warehouses eclipse the payrolls of unskilled warehouse workers. It’s not just Walmart. Amazon is also going to incredible lengths to automate its warehouses, creating what market-intelligence firm Interact Analysis’ Rueben Scriven told the amounts to an “arms race” between retailers. Yet despite major financial commitments, many of these efforts are crumbling. Case in point, Kroger had to write off a whopping $2.6 billion after a major investment in an “ automated fulfillment network” failed to pay off Meanwhile, a far more ambitious transition to humanoid warehouse robots feels like even more of a stretch. While companies are into the development of bipedal bots, the tech largely remains a Moonshot for practical physical labor. Robots Are About to Outnumber Humans At Amazon Warehouses

"More Bullish or More Bearish". How would I view the technicals for the Mag 7 stocks. This week we got a sneak-peak at the playbook for when
articles.content: US stocks close higher; Nasdaq gains for fourth straight week Week ahead: US inflation and retail sales lead a busy economic calendar. Be aware. Let's Play... "More Bullish or More Bearish". How would I view the technicals for the Mag 7 stocks. This week we got a sneak-peak at the playbook for when the AI bubble bursts What's open and closed in US and Canadian markets on Monday Bakers Hughes total rig count +5 to 603 European stocks finish higher Friday, but most post weekly declines SpaceX lockup expiration puts buyers to the test. The technicals define the risk. JPMorgan: The G7’s 100 million barrel oil release is mostly old barrels with a new bow on it Broader stock indices bouncing modestly. Support near 100 hour MAs held yesterday US October UMich prelim consumer sentiment 46.3 vs 47.8 expected Bitcoin sellers had their shot. They missed. Canada September employment change -68.3K vs +9.2K expected Morning Kickstart: Dollar mixed, stocks rebound and oil retreats amid Iran uncertainty Bessent hires former Fed board nominee and investingLive reader, Judy Shelton as adviser investingLive European session wrap: Stocks rebound as bond market nerves ease, for now How have interest rate expectations changed after this week's events? U.S. stock buyers had a better day on Friday. After Thursday’s selling tied to concerns over AI revenues, all five major indices finished higher, with the Dow leading the percentage gains. The economic news was less encouraging. U.S. consumer sentiment disappointed while inflation expectations edged higher. Canada lost another 68,300 jobs, pushing the Canadian dollar lower. Nevertheless, stocks, precious metals and Bitcoin all advanced into the weekend. Dollar mixed; Canadian dollar hurt by employment report The dollar finished mixed. It was strongest against the Canadian dollar and Japanese yen, gaining about 0.25% against each, and weakest against the Australian dollar. The late-session snapshot of the major currency pairs showed: EURUSD: 1.1201, −0.07%. USDJPY: 158.26, +0.25%. GBPUSD: 1.3233, +0.07%. USDCHF: 0.8300, −0.17%. USDCAD: 1.4261, +0.25%. AUDUSD: 0.6985, +0.43%. NZDUSD: 0.5613, +0.05%. USDCAD jumped from around 1.4232 before the Canadian employment report to near 1.4293 afterward. Some of that gain was retraced, but the Canadian dollar remained under pressure. Treasury curve flattens Treasury yields were mixed near the close, with shorter maturities moving higher while the 30-year yield edged lower: 2-year: 4.7911%, +3.51 basis points. 5-year: 5.0211%, +3.01 basis points. 10-year: 5.2441%, +1.11 basis points. 30-year: 5.6001%, −0.69 basis point. That combination flattened the curve. The rise in near-term inflation expectations gave traders another reason to remain cautious about the inflation outlook, even with consumer sentiment weakening. U.S. stocks finish higher The major indices closed higher across the board: Dow industrial average: 51,660.18, +423.06 points or +0.83%. S&P 500: 7,811.54, +46.18 points or +0.59%. Nasdaq Composite: 27,366.17, +172.83 points or +0.64%. Russell 2000: 2,806.9815, +12.8535 points or +0.46%. Nasdaq 100: 30,883.15, +157.34 points or +0.51%. The rebound extended beyond technology, with the Dow outperforming and small caps also participating. Still, one positive session does not remove the questions surrounding AI spending, revenues and valuations. In Adam’s afternoon review, he highlighted that Thursday’s OpenAI revenue comparison required an adjustment for partner revenue. He also noted that the dollar fell alongside AI shares during the initial reaction—an unusual response for a currency that often benefits when risk assets decline. That relationship bears watching. It's European stocks also finished Friday higher: Germany’s DAX: 25,087.28, +1.13%. France’s CAC: 7,803.34, +0.95%. UK’s FTSE 100: 10,552.04, +1.06%. Spain’s IBEX: 19,033.10, +0.55%. Italy’s FTSE MIB: 49,746.30, +0.91%. Friday’s gains were not enough to erase weekly losses in most markets. Italy fell 1.46%, France declined 1.19%, Germany lost 0.57% and Spain slipped 0.27%. The UK bucked the trend with a 0.86% gain. French unrest and fiscal uncertainty remained part of the European backdrop. See the European close review here. Michigan sentiment falls; inflation expectations rise The preliminary October University of Michigan consumer sentiment index fell to 46.3 from 48.1, below the 47.8 estimate. Current conditions were particularly weak at 44.7 versus 51.0 expected. Expectations were better than forecast at 47.3 versus 45.5. For the Fed, the inflation expectations figures remain the concern: One-year expectations: 4.7%, up from 4.6%. Five-year expectations: 3.5%, up from 3.4%. Consumers are feeling worse, but they are also expecting higher prices. That is an uncomfortable combination for policymakers, but is the fear greater than the reality? The headline was deeply depressed, although it remained above the 44.8 May low cited in the report. Next week, we get CPI and PPI data which combined will help to calculate the PCE. Canada loses another 68.3K jobs Canada’s September employment report missed expectations for a 9.2K increase with a sharp decline of 68.3K. Following August’s 41.7K decline, the two-month loss reached 110K. Full-time employment fell 35,400 and part-time employment declined 32,900. The unemployment rate rose to 6.5% from 6.4%, while participation slipped to 64.8% from 65.0%. The participation decline limited the increase in unemployment. There were some qualifications to the weak headline. Public-sector employment fell 70,000, while private-sector employment rose 24,100. Education and youth employment declines also raised questions about seasonal adjustments around the return to school. Nevertheless, another large employment decline is difficult to ignore. Permanent employees’ wage growth also increased to 2.3% from 2.0%, adding a complication for the Bank of Canada. Oil little changed; Iran remains a weekend risk WTI crude futures were near $91.50 in the supplied snapshot, up $0.01 or 0.01%. Earlier relief followed President Trump’s comments that discussions with Iran were productive and that attacks on Tehran would be deferred until after the midterm elections. That helped reduce the immediate escalation premium, but it did not resolve the conflict or the risks to energy supplies. The afternoon Baker Hughes report showed total U.S. rigs rising by 5 to 603, including a 6-rig increase in oil rigs to 462. Gold and silver advance Precious metals posted solid gains in the late-session snapshot: Spot gold: $4,196.065, +$62.375 or +1.51%. Silver: $60.7912, +$1.6107 or +2.72%. Gold advanced despite higher 2-, 5- and 10-year yields. The mixed dollar and slightly lower 30-year yield offered a less uniform headwind, but the strength in metals also suggests demand extended beyond a simple interest-rate trade. Rising inflation expectations may have contributed, although the snapshot alone cannot establish the driver. Bitcoin edges higher Bitcoin traded near $82,316, up $640 or 0.78%. The gain was consistent with the recovery in equities. It was a better day for risk assets, although Bitcoin’s move did not establish a separate trend from broader markets. See the latest technically HERE. What carries into next week? Stocks recovered, but inflation concerns and questions over AI economics remain. Canadian employment weakness adds another issue for currency traders, while Middle East headlines retain the potential to change the mood over the weekend. Monday brings a split holiday session: U.S. stocks will trade normally, the U.S. bond market will be closed, and Canadian markets will close for Thanksgiving. That leaves traders facing potentially thinner conditions as the new week begins. See what’s open and closed here. This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.
